claims.text: Mechanical wear continuously ruptures a protective oxide or passive film on the more reactive intermetallic phases.
Oxide-film rupture exposes fresh phase surfaces during each contact cycle.
Freshly exposed intermetallic surfaces drive localized galvanic corrosion at elevated temperature.
The coupled process produces more total mass loss than isolated wear or corrosion.
A eutectic or hypereutectic HEA coating can contain an FCC matrix and dispersed sigma phase.
The relevant multiphase alloy contains mechanically distinct soft and hard phases selected from FCC, B2, Laves, and sigma phases.
The initial alloy surface has a protective oxide scale produced by high-temperature exposure.
Sliding or abrasive contact in a corrosive environment near 600 °C permits repeated oxide formation and rupture.
A chloride or acidic molten-salt environment at approximately 600 °C is an applicable boundary condition for the proposed process.
Compositionally distinct phases form microgalvanic couples because they have different electrochemical potentials.
Removal of the oxide film activates localized galvanic cells between phases with different corrosion susceptibilities.
Localized electrochemical dissolution weakens matrix–intermetallic interfaces.
Interface weakening accelerates both mechanical and corrosion-assisted material removal beyond the sum of isolated wear and corrosion.
Corrosion current density increases during simultaneous wear-corrosion relative to corrosion-only exposure.
Wear rate increases during simultaneous wear-corrosion relative to wear-only exposure.
Total degradation under simultaneous wear-corrosion is super-additive relative to the sum of separate wear and corrosion losses.
A critical temperature in the range of approximately 400–600 °C governs the onset of strong oxide-disruption synergy.
The synergy is weaker below the critical temperature, in non-aggressive environments, or in single-phase and compositionally uniform alloys.

contradictions.description: The predicted-outcome field permits comparison with a test conducted without elevated temperature, whereas the defined baseline requires isolated wear and corrosion tests at the same temperature. These are not equivalent matched baselines.
